extraction.name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
extraction.description: POPE is an evaluation method and benchmark designed to evaluate object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). It formulates object hallucination evaluation as a binary classification task by prompting models with closed-ended Yes-or-No probing questions about ground-truth and negative objects under Random, Popular, and Adversarial sampling settings.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: POPE constructs evaluation triples each consisting of an image, multiple questions, and binary Yes/No answers. Ground-truth objects are extracted from existing dataset annotations or automatic segmentation tools like SEEM. For nonexistent objects, negative sampling is performed under three settings: Random Sampling, Popular Sampling (selecting top frequent dataset objects), and Adversarial Sampling (selecting frequent co-occurring objects with ground-truth objects). For evaluation on MSCOCO, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects were randomly selected from the validation set, constructing 6 polling questions per image with a 1:1 ground-truth to nonexistent object ratio.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and object annotations sampled from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images with more than 3 ground-truth objects were filtered from the MSCOCO validation set. The ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects was set to 1:1 for label balance. Polling questions were constructed using templated queries such as 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?' with corresponding 'Yes' or 'No' ground truth labels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth object labels were gathered from human annotations in original datasets or automatically generated using the SEEM segmentation tool. Polling questions and Yes/No labels were programmatically built using predefined question templates paired with ground-truth objects and sampled negative objects.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once), ChatGPT
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment (e.g., autonomous driving systems making wrong decisions due to an incorrect understanding of the external environment). Evaluating and mitigating hallucination contributes to developing more reliable and human-aligned models.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The visual instruction datasets constructed based on MSCOCO contain an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part. LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing or co-occurring objects, and exhibit overconfidence by heavily leaning toward answering 'Yes'.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark only focuses on coarse-grained object hallucinations, not covering fine-grained hallucinations (e.g., number, attributes, positions) or overall LVLM capacity. Evaluation was limited to subsets of validation sets due to computational constraints. The matching-based method to parse 'Yes' or 'No' may fail when LVLMs provide open-ended responses lacking explicit keywords. Automatic segmentation tools (SEEM) may diverge from human annotations.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs).
